html:
In 1990 Prime Minister V. P. Singh announced that India would reserve 27 percent of central government jobs for the "Other Backward Classes", following the report of the Mandal Commission. It was one of the biggest changes in Indian politics since independence.

The commission was set up in 1979 under Morarji Desai and led by the politician B. P. Mandal. Its 1980 report found that the backward castes, above the Dalits in the caste order but far below the upper castes, made up about half the population yet held few state jobs. The report sat unused for ten years.

The announcement set off fierce protests by upper caste students, some of whom set themselves on fire. In 1992 the Supreme Court upheld the quota but capped all reservations at half of the posts. Mandal reshaped politics in north India, raising parties built on backward caste votes, while the rival politics of the temple at Ayodhya rose at the same time; see Babri Masjid demolished.
